prompt: Reserved concurrency or provisioned concurrency: which one fixes our slow first requests?
persona: a startup founder in office hours
ten_second: Provisioned concurrency. It keeps environments initialized, so first requests skip the cold start. Reserved concurrency only sets capacity aside and caps it.
sixty_second: Both control concurrency. The difference is that only provisioned concurrency removes cold starts.
It works like this. A cold start is the time Lambda needs to prepare a new environment.
Provisioned concurrency keeps some environments initialized before requests arrive.
So the first requests get an answer in double-digit milliseconds.
Reserved concurrency sets aside part of the account limit for one function and caps it.
It costs nothing extra, but it doesn't prepare any environment.
The thing to watch is cost. You pay for provisioned environments even when they're idle.
And you set it on a published version or an alias, not on the latest version.
Application Auto Scaling can change it on a schedule.
In your case, keep it high in busy hours and low at night.
When do the slow requests happen: after quiet nights, or at a known time each morning?

key_points.point: Provisioned concurrency is a number of pre-initialized execution environments, so a function using it does not exhibit cold start behavior.
accept: it prepares environments before the requests arrive

key_points.point: Reserved concurrency reserves a subset of the account concurrency limit for a function and caps it there; it incurs no additional charges.
accept: reserved concurrency is a cap and costs nothing

key_points.point: You pay for provisioned instances even when they are not handling requests.
accept: provisioned concurrency costs money while idle
we pay for warm environments all the time

key_points.point: Provisioned concurrency must be applied to a specific version or alias of a function, not the $LATEST version.
accept: set it on a version or an alias

key_points.point: Application Auto Scaling can adjust provisioned concurrency on a schedule or in real time as demand changes.
accept: scale it with Application Auto Scaling

must_not_say.error: reserved concurrency keeps the functions warm
must_not_say.correct: Reserved concurrency reserves part of the account concurrency and caps the function. Provisioned concurrency keeps environments initialized.
You pay for the provisioned instances even when they are not handling requests.

must_not_say.error: turn it on for the latest version of the function
must_not_say.correct: Provisioned concurrency must be applied to a specific version or alias of a function, not the $LATEST version.

follow_ups.question: What happens when traffic goes above the provisioned amount?
follow_ups.answer: Lambda can scale the function above the provisioned concurrency setting. The excess executions are billed at the on-demand rate, and they run in new environments, which can have a cold start.

follow_ups.question: Could SnapStart fix the slow first requests instead?
follow_ups.answer: SnapStart reduces startup latency, but it is a best-effort optimization and does not guarantee the end of cold starts. For strict double-digit millisecond startup times, AWS recommends provisioned concurrency.

prompt: If no calls arrive at night, do we still pay for the functions?
ten_second: No, not for the functions. We pay per request and for how long the code runs. With no work at night, they cost nothing.
sixty_second: The short answer is no, not for the functions themselves.
It works like this. A function is a small piece of our code that AWS runs when work arrives.
AWS charges for each request and for how long the code runs.
When no upload arrives, nothing runs, and we don't pay for idle capacity.
So a quiet night costs almost nothing for this part.
The thing to watch is any extra we add for speed.
If we keep functions ready for speed, we pay for that even when nothing runs.
And the queue, the database and the storage still have their own costs at night.
In your case, the busy morning gets the capacity it needs, and the night stays cheap.
Is a short delay on the first upload of the morning fine for our customers?

key_points.point: Lambda functions are priced on the number of requests served and on the duration the code runs, measured in GB-seconds.
accept: we pay per request and per run time
the bill counts requests and duration

key_points.point: You pay only for actual function invocations and execution time, and you do not provision or pay for idle capacity.
accept: we don't pay for idle capacity

key_points.point: Provisioned concurrency increases costs: you pay for the provisioned instances even when they are not handling requests.
accept: keeping functions ready costs money all night
warm functions are charged while idle

key_points.point: AWS Lambda is priced on a pay-per-use basis.
accept: we pay for what we use

must_not_say.correct: Lambda is priced on a pay-per-use basis: we pay for the requests and for the duration the code runs.

must_not_say.error: the functions can never cost us anything at night
must_not_say.correct: Functions with provisioned concurrency are charged even when they are not handling requests.

follow_ups.question: Is there a free amount each month?
follow_ups.answer: Yes. The Lambda free tier includes one million requests and 400,000 GB-seconds per month. The free tier does not apply to functions that use provisioned concurrency.

follow_ups.question: Can a commitment lower the daytime bill for the functions?
follow_ups.answer: Yes. Compute Savings Plans apply to Lambda usage automatically. EC2 Instance Savings Plans and Reserved Instances do not apply to Lambda.
